column3: It directly repeats the assignment of a distinct rite to every community, making it the closest parallel to the focus.
The challenge about whether punishment is magic does not develop rites, provision, oneness, or submission.
Its humble turning to the Lord supports the focus's call to receptive humility, though not its ritual setting.
It directly joins naming Allah with livestock He provided during appointed ritual days.
The immediate context identifies honoring Allah's sacred rites as piety of the hearts.
It depicts surrender to Allah when fabricated claims collapse, but in a final judgment setting.
It explicitly announces that God is one, a central declaration of the focus verse.
Its immediate livestock and anti-idolatry instruction frames the sacrificial practice developed in the focus.
The disciples' declaration that they are Muslims provides a direct but general instance of submission.
It immediately explains that sacrifice reaches Allah through piety and praise rather than flesh or blood.
It treats livestock as divine provision for material use, without the naming or ritual dimension.
The naming of a future messenger does not clarify invocation of Allah's name in worship.
It couples one God with exclusive worship, closely supporting the focus's oneness and submission.
The preceding verse establishes the animals' benefits and their destination at the ancient House.
It requires mentioning Allah's name over food obtained through hunting, closely paralleling the focus's food-and-name relation.
It condemns invented rules about livestock and failure to name Allah over them, a close corrective parallel.
The description of punishment affecting bodies does not develop the focus's themes.
It presents all creatures before Allah, the One and the Overpowering, reinforcing exclusive divine authority.
It expressly declares one God and commands people to direct themselves rightly to Him.
It rejects worship of others and commands submission to the Lord of all worlds.
Its hearts humbly yield after recognizing truth, directly developing the focus's closing address to the humble.
It explains differentiated communal paths under Allah's will, closely paralleling distinct rites for communities.
The immediate continuation describes the humble as hearts moved by Allah's mention, patient, prayerful, and charitable from provision.
It joins a submitting community with being shown its rites, directly paralleling both dimensions of the focus.
Its allocation of heirs to every person shares only the broad language of divine assignment.
Its concern with hearts able to understand is only a broad counterpart to the focus's humble-hearted audience.
It directly states that the audience's God is one.
It establishes the permissibility of grazing livestock, supplying the legal provision background for the focus.
The rebuke for worldly exultation does not clarify the focus's ritual or theological claims.
The prohibition on insulting labels concerns social conduct, not invocation of Allah's name.
It identifies provision as Allah's differentiated gift, though without ritual naming or sacrifice.
It immediately commands naming Allah over sacrificial animals and sharing their meat.
The repeated greeting of peace does not develop submission to the one God.
Its distribution of rain for remembrance provides only a general pattern of divine gifts prompting remembrance.
It identifies the community as Muslims and commands worship, extending the focus's submission theme within the same surah.
It directly declares that God is one and alone deserving of worship.
It combines Allah's sole divinity with livestock granted to humanity, though it lacks the ritual naming relation.
The movement of mountains on the Last Day does not develop the focus's themes.
It directly combines the declaration of one God with the question of whether people will submit.
It mentions Quranic reminders but does not specify rites, livestock, oneness, or submission.
The condemnation of one who turns aside to mislead does not clarify the focus verse.
The command to glorify the Lord's name supports the focus's invocation of Allah's name.
Its statement that every community has an appointed term shares only the communal grouping.
Its call to attentive hearts and listening is a distant counterpart to receptivity and remembrance.
It links Allah as provider with the command to be among those who submit to Him.
It defines submission of one's face to Allah and presents it as the path of guidance for others.
The challenge about a ladder for listening to heaven does not illuminate the focus.
The believers' increased faith and submission under trial provides a contextual example of trusting surrender.
It identifies livestock as Allah's provision for riding and eating, without the focus's ritual use.
The promise of gardens for believers does not clarify communal rites or submission.
Its command to glorify the Lord's name is a general parallel to the focus's naming of Allah.
Its recognition of distinct directions and call to excel in good supports differentiated communal practice under divine authority.
The judgment-scene reproach for rejecting faith does not develop the focus's particular themes.
It protects places where Allah's name is much mentioned, linking divine naming to communal worship.
It joins faith with spending from the provision Allah gave, a partial parallel to provision acknowledged before God.
The ruined town, abandoned well, and lofty palace do not develop the focus's themes.
It identifies the saved believers as those who were Muslims, giving a general parallel to submission.
It condemns falsely prohibiting the provision Allah gave, closely supporting the focus's attribution of livestock provision to Him.
The contrast between calling to salvation and the Fire does not clarify rites or submission.
The command to enter Paradise in peace does not develop the focus's submission language.
It assigns a messenger to every community, offering a general counterpart to community-specific divine ordering.
The creation and resurrection argument does not develop the focus's ritual, naming, or submission themes.
The distinctive personal name of Yahya is unrelated to invocation of Allah's name.
Its command to give believers good news echoes the focus's closing command but adds no shared rationale.
The command to eat and drink in Paradise does not clarify livestock provision or ritual naming.
The merciful greeting of peace in Paradise is not a parallel to submission or ritual remembrance.
Its good news and Paradise provision are broadly compatible with the focus's final encouragement, but not directly linked.
The duration of Hell does not develop any focus theme.
It declares Allah the One and the Overpowering while rejecting divine offspring, reinforcing uncompromising oneness.
Its hunting test concerns regulated access to game, but not naming Allah or communal rites.
The description of reclining in Paradise does not develop the focus.
It directly commands remembering Allah after completing rites, closely paralleling the focus's communal rite and divine remembrance.
Its command to give believers good news echoes only the focus's concluding encouragement.
The magicians ask to die as Muslims, presenting submission to Allah under severe pressure.
Its command to give glad tidings to the patient only broadly corresponds to the focus's encouragement of the humble.
The formula in Allah's name shows His name authorizing a message, though outside sacrificial worship.
It corrects divided conceptions of God by affirming that Allah is one and uniquely sovereign.
Their forced surrender on the Day of Judgment is a contrast to the focus's commanded voluntary submission.
It distinguishes claimed submission from Allah's guidance to faith, clarifying that submission is not a human achievement to boast of.
The condemned offer surrender when confronted by angels, a negative final-judgment counterpart to the focus's command.
Its peaceful Paradise and regular provision are only remotely related to the focus's provision theme.
The queen's confession of submission to Allah, Lord of the worlds, directly illustrates the focus's final command.
It directly commands regular remembrance of the Lord's name, though without a ritual-food context.
Naming the spring Salsabil does not clarify naming Allah in worship.
It joins remembering the Lord's name with prayer, a general liturgical parallel.
It directly records the command to submit and Abraham's immediate submission to the Lord of all worlds.
The differing degrees assigned for deeds do not develop the focus's communal or ritual claims.
The demand to come in submission is political and does not itself name submission to Allah.
The command to glorify the Lord's name gives a general parallel to invoking Allah's name.
It contrasts aversion to mention of Allah alone with delight in others, strongly clarifying the focus's one-God orientation.
The testimony of skins at judgment does not develop the focus's rites, provision, or submission.
It forbids eating what lacks Allah's name and ties that practice to idolatry, closely matching the focus's livestock-and-name relation.
The declaration of belief in Allah alone rejects former association, though it comes only after punishment is seen.
It defines full submission as accepting the messenger's judgment inwardly and outwardly, a general but robust parallel.
Jacob's response to a false account does not develop the focus's themes.
It grounds worship in Allah's sole lordship over heaven and earth and denies any equal to His name.
Its concern with false hearing and distortion of judgment does not clarify the focus.
It contrasts fabricating lies about Allah with being called to Islam, supporting the focus's call to submission.
Jonah's rescue of believers does not develop the focus's ritual or theological elements.
It rejects humanly invented divine names without authority, sharply contrasting the focus's naming of the one true God.
It directly joins surrendering one's whole self to Allah with righteous action, closely matching the focus's command to submit.
Jacob's family declares that it will worship one God and be submitting to Him, directly combining oneness, communal identity, and submission.
It commands completion of Hajj and Umrah and regulates sacrificial offerings, supplying the ritual setting of the focus.
It frames Hajj as appointed months with prescribed conduct and remembrance, a close ritual counterpart.
It commands remembrance of Allah on numbered pilgrimage days, extending the focus's rite-and-remembrance pattern.
It states that the religion with Allah is submission, directly grounding the focus's imperative to submit.
It declares that all in heaven and earth submit to Allah willingly or unwillingly, placing the focus's command in universal divine sovereignty.
It identifies Islam as the accepted religion, directly reinforcing the focus's call to submit.
It praises the one who submits his face to Allah while doing good, a close formulation of the focus's final command.
It commands respect for Allah's sacred symbols and sacrificial offerings, directly related to the focus's communal rite.
It forbids animals sacrificed in a name other than Allah's, directly sharpening the focus's requirement to name Allah over livestock.
It rejects invented livestock consecrations, a close corrective counterpart to the focus's God-given ritual order.
It commands eating that over which Allah's name has been mentioned, directly repeating the focus's food-and-name relation.
It explains why food named for Allah may be eaten and distinguishes what He has forbidden, directly extending the same rule.
It condemns assigning shares of crops and livestock to Allah and invented partners, sharply clarifying the focus's one-God attribution.
It identifies livestock as Allah's provision and commands eating from what He has provided, supplying the focus's provision premise.
It declares that prayer, sacrifice, life, and death belong to Allah alone, a direct synthesis of sacrifice and divine oneness.
It denies any partner to Allah and identifies submission as the commanded response, directly echoing the focus's conclusion.
It commands sincere devotion to Allah at every place of worship, a general parallel to exclusive communal worship.
Noah states that he has been commanded to be among those who submit, providing a prophetic instance of the focus's command.
Moses tells believers to rely on Allah if they are Muslims, linking faith with active submission.
Joseph asks to die as one submitted to Allah, extending submission as a lifelong orientation.
It commands eating lawful good provision from Allah with gratitude, a general counterpart to the focus's provided livestock.
It forbids what has been dedicated to other than Allah, directly contrasting with the focus's naming of Allah over animals.
It rejects human declarations that distort what Allah has made lawful or forbidden, a corrective to invented food rules.
It commands calling upon Allah by His beautiful names, supporting the focus's invocation of Allah's name in worship.
Allah declares His sole divinity and commands worship and prayer for His remembrance, closely linking oneness and remembrance.
It states that every messenger was sent with the declaration that there is no god but Allah and the command to worship Him.
It summons people to Hajj, directly supplying the pilgrimage context for the focus's communal sacrificial rite.
It commands pilgrims to complete their rites and vows and circumambulate the ancient House, immediately continuing the same ritual sequence.
It commands exclusive devotion to Allah and rejection of association, directly reinforcing the focus's one-God declaration.
It identifies the believers as one community under one Lord and commands worship of Him, closely paralleling the focus's communal orientation under one God.
It declares that the believers' God and the others' God is one and that they are submitting to Him.
It commands steadfast orientation to the religion Allah established, a broader counterpart to submitting to the one God.
It describes surrendering one's face to Allah while doing good as taking hold of the firmest bond.
It requires believers to yield personal choice when Allah and His messenger decide, clarifying submission as obedience.
It commands worship of Allah with religion sincerely devoted to Him, reinforcing exclusive submission.
It explicitly commands turning to the Lord and submitting to Him before punishment, a direct parallel to the focus's imperative.
It praises one who calls to Allah, acts rightly, and declares membership among the Muslims.
It describes Allah's ordained religion for the communities of earlier messengers, supporting the focus's communal religious ordering.
Jesus declares that Allah is his Lord and the audience's Lord and commands worship of Him, reinforcing one shared divine authority.
It distinguishes outward submission from settled faith, clarifying that Islam can be named before faith fully enters the heart.
It refers to the single household of Muslims saved from Lot's town, offering only a narrative instance of submission.
It distinguishes Muslims who seek right guidance from those who deviate, extending the focus's call to submit.
It commands sincere worship of Allah, prayer, and almsgiving within the upright religion, a strong general parallel to the focus's exclusive worship.
Abraham and Jacob charge their descendants not to die except as Muslims, extending submission across the community and generations.
It commands believers to enter into submission completely, reinforcing the focus's imperative to submit wholly to Allah.
The disciples identify themselves as Muslims, providing another communal instance of submission without the focus's ritual dimension.
It calls communities to worship none but Allah, associate nothing with Him, and avoid human lords, directly reinforcing exclusive divine authority.
It commands worship of Allah and association of nothing with Him, directly supporting the focus's one-God declaration.
It rejects calling on others besides Allah and states that people are commanded to submit to the Lord of all worlds.
Abraham turns wholly to the Creator of heaven and earth as a hanif and denies association, closely supporting exclusive submission.
It identifies the straight religion as Abraham's upright way, placing the focus's rite within its Abrahamic religious frame.
Pharaoh's late claim to believe in the one God and be Muslim is a negative, compelled counterpart to the focus's command to submit.
It concludes the challenge to deniers by asking whether they will submit, offering a direct imperative parallel.
It states the command to worship Allah and not associate partners with Him, closely supporting the focus's exclusive worship.
It commands following Abraham's upright religion and rejects association, reinforcing the Abrahamic monotheism behind the pilgrimage rites.
Noah commands his people to worship Allah alone because they have no other god, directly expressing the focus's one-God premise.
It commands worship of the Lord of the sacred city and submission to Him, linking sacred place, worship, and Islam.
It attributes rain and the revival of earth to Allah, offering only a broad provision-and-gratitude counterpart.
Its inclusion of Muslim men and women gives a broad communal picture of submission without the focus's ritual content.
It asks why one should not worship the Creator to whom all return, reinforcing the focus's exclusive orientation to God.
It commands worshipping Allah with religion sincerely devoted to Him, directly strengthening the focus's exclusive submission.
It commands worship of Allah alone and gratitude to Him, directly relating devotion to the giver of provision.
